title: Live Polls for a TV Show
prompt: A TV show asks viewers a question on air, and viewers vote in the show's app during a 60-second window; the result is shown on screen right after. Design the voting system, using the full routine.
facts: About 2 million viewers vote in each poll; measured at earlier polls, the busiest second brings about 100,000 votes, and the app servers admit at most 120,000 votes per second
A vote counts if an app server receives it before the window closes, by the servers' clock; phones send at once and retry with the same vote ID for up to 2 seconds
Each vote is one small request from a logged-in viewer; a viewer may vote once per poll, and tapping again must not count twice
An app server handles about 5,000 vote requests per second

An in-memory store can run a small script atomically on one node: "if (poll, viewer) is not marked, mark it and add 1 to this node's counter for the option". A node runs about 50,000 such scripts per second, and acknowledges only after its replica has the change; if a node fails, its replica takes over within 2 seconds

A message queue takes about 200,000 messages per second and delivers within 1 second; queue consumers can apply about 150,000 votes per second in total with the same script; the database handles about 5,000 writes per second
Requirement: every vote sent within the window from a logged-in viewer is counted exactly once in effect
Requirement: the final result is shown within 5 seconds after the window closes; the system keeps working if one app server or one store node fails
scope: Collecting and counting votes for one poll at a time
Showing the result on the TV screen is out of scope

requirements: States one vote per viewer per poll, the 60-second window, the result within 5 seconds of closing, and survival of one server or store node failure
estimation: Peak votes: the measured busiest second, about 100,000, against an average of 2 million ÷ 60 ≈ 33,000; admission caps it at 120,000
App servers: 120,000 ÷ 5,000 = 24 at the cap, plus spares; store nodes: 120,000 ÷ 50,000 = 2.4, so 3 plus replicas; why the database alone (5,000 writes per second) cannot take the peak
design: API (a vote call returning accepted), data model (one record per viewer per poll, a counter per option), a high-level design with a fast path for the peak, and a deep dive on counting each viewer once
data: One atomic step marks the viewer and counts the vote together on one node, so a failure cannot do one without the other; viewers are spread over nodes, each node keeps its own counter per option, and the result is the sum
Where the final counts come from and how they are kept after the poll
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: if a store node fails, its replica takes over and votes in the last moment may need replaying from the queue; counting through a queue is safer but adds a few seconds; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, count in the in-memory store: `POST /polls/{id}/votes {option, voteId}` returns 202 after the store acknowledges. 24 app servers plus spares for the 120,000 cap. Viewers are spread over 3 store nodes by viewer ID; on its node, each vote runs the atomic script that marks the viewer and adds 1 to that node's counter for the option, so marking and counting cannot be split, and no single counter takes every vote. 3 × 50,000 = 150,000 scripts per second, above the 120,000 cap. A retried vote finds the mark and changes nothing. At close, the app waits 2 seconds for retries, then sums the 3 nodes' counters: within 5 seconds, even if a replica took over (2 seconds). A background job copies the marks to the database at 5,000 per second for records. Failures: the load balancer skips a dead app server; a node's replica holds every acknowledged vote and takes over within 2 seconds, and phones retry unacknowledged ones. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: the counts live in memory until copied.

Design B, count from a queue: the vote call puts (poll, viewer, option, voteId) on a queue and returns 202 once the queue has it; up to 120,000 per second, under its 200,000. Consumers apply each vote with the same atomic script on the store (mark the viewer and add to that node's counter), and only then mark the batch done in the queue. A replayed batch finds the marks and changes nothing, so a vote is never lost or counted twice. Consumers apply 150,000 per second, above the 120,000 cap, so at close the backlog is about 1 second of delivery plus under a second of applying; the app waits 2 seconds for phone retries and 1 more for the queue, then sums the counters: within 5 seconds. Failures: a dead consumer's batch is delivered again; a store node's replica takes over within 2 seconds. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: one more moving part, and results lag a second or two behind the votes.

assumptions: The phone gives each vote an ID and retries with it
reference.design:
Requirements: one vote per logged-in viewer per poll, counted if received before the window closes, result within 5 seconds after closing, survive one app server or store node failure. Out of scope: the TV graphics.
Estimates: the busiest second brings about 100,000 votes (average 33,000), capped at 120,000. 24 app servers at 5,000 each, plus spares; 3 store nodes at 50,000 scripts each. The database's 5,000 writes per second cannot take the peak.
API: POST /polls/{id}/votes {option, voteId} → 202; GET /polls/{id}/result. Data: in the in-memory store, viewers are spread over 3 nodes; each node holds a mark per (poll, viewer) and its own counter per option; later, a votes table in the database.
Design and deep dive: on the viewer's node, one atomic script marks the viewer and adds 1 to that node's counter for the option, so a crash cannot mark without counting or count without marking. A retried vote finds the mark and changes nothing. Each option is counted on all 3 nodes, so no single counter is hot; 150,000 scripts per second cover the 120,000 cap. At close, the app waits 2 seconds for retries and sums the 3 nodes' counters, within 5 seconds.
Failures: the load balancer skips a dead app server; a node acknowledges only after its replica has the change, so the replica, taking over within 2 seconds, holds every acknowledged vote, and phones retry the rest with the same vote ID. Summary: each requirement is met; the marks are copied to the database afterwards.
alternatives: Count from a queue: safer replay, a couple of seconds of lag
Rejected: writing every vote straight to the database, because the peak of 100,000 per second is twenty times its 5,000

title: Free Parking Spaces in a City
prompt: A city puts a sensor in every space of its public garages and wants an app that shows how many spaces are free in each garage. Design it, using the full routine.
facts: 100 garages with 40,000 spaces in total; each sensor reports an event when a car arrives or leaves, about 200 events per second at rush hour
A sensor resends an event until the system acknowledges it, so the same event can arrive more than once; each event carries the sensor ID and an event number that grows for that sensor
Up to 3,000 app requests per second at rush hour, each asking for the free-space counts of the garages near the user; the cache handles about 50,000 reads per second at about 1 ms each
The database handles about 2,000 writes per second; a queue, if used, keeps events for 1 day and delivers within 1 second
Requirement: while the database and cache are working, a change in a garage shows in the app within 30 seconds; during an outage, affected garages show "may be out of date"
Requirement: a repeated event never changes a count twice
Requirement: if a garage has sent nothing for 5 minutes, the app shows its count as "may be out of date"; events are kept for 30 days
scope: Counting free spaces and showing them in the app
Payment and reservations are out of scope

requirements: States 30-second freshness, repeated events counted once, the 5-minute out-of-date rule, and 30 days of events
estimation: Writes: 200 events per second, under the database's 2,000
Storage: 200 × about 100 bytes × 86,400 ≈ 1.7 GB a day, about 52 GB for 30 days
Reads: 3,000 per second served from a cache, about 1 ms each
design: API for sensors and for the app, a data model with one row per space and a count per garage, a high-level design, and a deep dive on applying each event once
data: Applying an event only if its number is higher than the last one stored for that sensor, and changing the garage count only if the space's occupied value actually changes
A durable current state per space (occupied, last event number) kept apart from the 30-day event log, so recovery never depends on old events
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: if the cache is lost, counts are read from the database until it fills again; a sensor that goes silent shows "may be out of date" after 5 minutes; caching for 10 seconds trades a little freshness for far fewer reads; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, write straight to the database: sensors call `POST /events {sensor, number, occupied}`; the server updates the space's row only if the event number is higher than the stored one, and in the same transaction changes the garage's free count by the difference between the old and new occupied value (none if unchanged); then it acknowledges. 200 writes per second, under 2,000. The app calls `GET /garages?near=…`, served from a cache refreshed every 10 seconds: 3,000 reads per second, under the cache's 50,000; a change shows within about 11 seconds. The cache keeps each garage's last event time with its count, and the server marks a garage "may be out of date" when answering, if that time is more than 5 minutes old. Events are also appended to a log table: about 52 GB for 30 days. Failures: if the cache fails, reads go to the database for a short time; if the database is down, sensors keep resending until it returns. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: one database does everything; simple, with room to spare at 200 writes per second.

Design B, a queue and counters in memory: sensors post events, which go on the queue (kept 1 day) and are acknowledged. Consumers apply each event to an in-memory record per space only if its number is higher, change the garage's free count only if the occupied value changed, then write each space's current state (occupied, last number) and the event log to the database in batches, and only after that mark the batch done in the queue. The app reads garage counts from memory, with each garage's last event time; a change shows within about 2 seconds (1 second delivery, under 1 second to apply). Failures: if the in-memory records are lost, they are rebuilt from the 40,000 current-state rows, which do not expire with the 30-day log, and the queue delivers again any batch not yet saved; the number check makes the replay harmless. Until rebuilt, garages show "may be out of date". Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: fresher counts, but more parts to run.

assumptions: Sensor clocks are not needed: event numbers order each sensor's events
Garages are few enough to list all counts near a user in one small response
reference.design:
Requirements: counts within 30 seconds of a change, repeated events counted once, "may be out of date" after 5 silent minutes, events kept 30 days. Out of scope: payments and reservations.
Estimates: 200 events per second at rush hour, under the database's 2,000 writes. Events: 200 × 100 bytes × 86,400 ≈ 1.7 GB a day, about 52 GB for 30 days. 3,000 app reads per second, from a cache.
API: POST /events {sensor, number, occupied} for sensors; GET /garages?near=… for the app. Data: spaces(sensor_id, garage_id, occupied, last_number); garages(id, free, last_event_at); an event log.
Design and deep dive: the server updates a space only if the event's number is higher than last_number, and in the same transaction changes the garage's free count by the difference between the old and new occupied value; a repeated or older event changes nothing, but is still acknowledged so the sensor stops resending. The spaces table is the current state and never expires; the event log is kept 30 days. A cache refreshed every 10 seconds answers 3,000 reads per second, under its 50,000, so changes show within about 11 seconds. The cache keeps each garage's last event time, and the server decides "may be out of date" when answering, so the 5-minute rule is applied exactly.
Failures: if the cache is lost, reads go to the database briefly; if the database is down, sensors keep resending and nothing is lost, and garages that stop updating show "may be out of date" after 5 minutes. Summary: each requirement is met with plenty of room.
alternatives: A queue with in-memory counters: fresher counts, more parts
Rejected: adding or subtracting from the garage count for every event without checking its number, because a resent event would change the count twice
